section.title: David Established in Jerusalem
section.sectionRationale: Set between the failed first attempt to bring the ark, chapter 13, and the corrected procession, chapter 15, this chapter pauses to show David's kingdom taking visible shape: Hiram of Tyre builds him a palace, his household grows, and, most importantly, David twice defeats the Philistines by directly inquiring of God rather than presuming on past victories. The chapter models dependent kingship, deliberately contrasted with Saul, who famously 'did not inquire of the LORD,' 10:14.
section.thesis: The LORD Himself establishes and exalts David's kingdom, and David's greatness is shown not in self-reliance but in repeatedly stopping to inquire of God before acting, a pattern of dependence that stands in sharp contrast to Saul's failure and models the kind of king, and the kind of people, God's covenant community is meant to be.
section.frameNote: Three beats: Hiram's gift and David's growing house, verses 1 to 7; the first Philistine victory at Baal-perazim after David inquires of God, verses 8 to 12; and the second victory after David inquires again and obeys God's precise battle plan, verses 13 to 17.

units.label: Hiram's gift and David's growing house
units.note: the LORD had established him as king

verses.text: Now Hiram king of Tyre sent envoys to David, along with cedar logs, stonemasons, and carpenters, to build a {{bayit|palace}} for him.
And David realized that the LORD had established him as king over Israel and had highly {{nasa|exalted}} his kingdom for the sake of His people Israel.
And David took more wives in Jerusalem and became the father of more sons and daughters.
These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,

units.label: The first victory: David inquires of God
units.note: should I go up against the Philistines

verses.text: When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over all Israel, they all went in search of him; but David learned of this and went out to face them.
Now the Philistines had come and raided the Valley of Rephaim.
So David {{darash|inquired}} of God, “Should I go up against the Philistines? Will You deliver them into my hand?” “Go,” replied the LORD, “for I will deliver them into your hand.”

So David and his men went up to Baal-perazim, where he defeated the Philistines and said, “Like a bursting flood, God has burst out against my enemies by my hand.” So they called that place Baal-perazim.
There the Philistines abandoned their gods, and David ordered that they be burned in the fire.

units.label: The second victory: David inquires again
units.note: David did as God had commanded him

verses.text: Once again the Philistines raided the valley.
So David again {{darash|inquired}} of God, who answered him, “Do not march up after them, but circle around them and attack them in front of the balsam trees.
As soon as you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move out to battle, because this will mean that God has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines.”
So David did as God had commanded him, and they struck down the army of the Philistines all the way from Gibeon to Gezer.
And David's fame went out into every land, and the LORD caused all nations to fear him.

bayit.gloss: House or, here, palace. Hiram's craftsmen build David a bayit of cedar in Jerusalem. The same word will govern the next several chapters: David wants to build the LORD a bayit, and the LORD instead promises to build David a bayit, a dynasty, 17:1-14.

nasa.gloss: To lift up, carry, bear, or exalt. Here it describes how the LORD 'highly exalted' David's kingdom, literally lifted it up. The same root describes the Levites carrying the ark on their shoulders in chapter 15; whether lifting up a king or bearing up God's presence, the word points to what only God can rightly raise or what only His appointed servants may rightly bear.

darash.gloss: To inquire, seek, or consult. David inquires of God twice in this chapter before going to battle, the very thing Saul famously failed to do, 10:14. The Chronicler consistently measures Israel's kings by whether they darash the LORD before acting.

basic.context: This chapter sits between the failed and corrected attempts to bring home the ark, chapters 13 and 15, and pauses to show David's kingdom taking shape under God's hand. Hiram, king of the great trading city of Tyre, sends cedar and craftsmen to build David a palace, a mark of international recognition. David's family grows in Jerusalem. Then the Philistines, who had tolerated Saul, move immediately against David once he is anointed over all Israel, raiding the Valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem. Twice David is attacked, and twice, rather than assuming he knows what to do, he stops and asks God directly whether and how to fight. Both times God answers, and both times David wins decisively, his fame spreading through every land.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative that doubles as a character study in dependent leadership. The chapter's key phrase, 'David inquired of God' (verse 10) and 'David again inquired of God' (verse 14), is placed by the Chronicler in deliberate contrast to the summary verdict on Saul: he died because he was unfaithful to the LORD and 'did not inquire of the LORD,' 10:13-14. The lesson is not a formula for guaranteed victory but a picture of a king, and a people, whose strength lies in humble dependence on God's direction rather than in past experience or self-confidence.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter's structure is built on two Hebrew roots. Nasa describes how the LORD 'highly exalted' David's kingdom, lifted it up, the same root that will describe the Levites lifting the ark on their shoulders in chapter 15; David's exaltation and the ark's proper handling are both, at root, about what God alone raises up or authorizes. And darash, to inquire or seek, appears twice as David asks God directly before each battle, the very verb whose absence condemned Saul, 10:14.
basic.typology: David inquiring of God before every battle, and receiving precise, situation-specific guidance, foreshadows the perfect, unbroken dependence of great David's greater Son, who said, 'I can do nothing on My own... I do not seek My own will but the will of Him who sent Me,' John 5:30. Where David's dependence was faithful but partial, Christ's was total.
basic.christ: David's pattern of inquiring of God rather than presuming on his own strength or past victories models the very dependence perfectly fulfilled in Jesus, who did nothing apart from the Father, John 5:19, 30. The kingdom that the LORD 'establishes' and 'exalts' for David here, verse 2, anticipates the greater exaltation of Christ, whom God has highly exalted and given the name above every name, Philippians 2:9, the true King before whom every enemy will finally be subdued.
basic.god: God is the one who actually establishes and exalts David's kingdom, 'for the sake of His people Israel,' not for David's own glory. He is also personally engaged and specific in guidance, not a distant force: He answers David's inquiries directly, with tactical detail, both permitting and directing the battle. God's aim throughout is His people's good and His own name being feared among the nations.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Chronicles 10:13-14 states that Saul died because he did not inquire of the LORD, the deliberate contrast this chapter sets up. 2 Samuel 5:17-25 records the same two Philistine battles in near-identical detail. John 5:19, 30 shows Christ's own total dependence on the Father. Philippians 2:9-11 speaks of God highly exalting Jesus, echoing the language of David's exaltation here.
basic.oneStory: Set between two ark narratives, this chapter shows the LORD building David's house and fame while David models the humble dependence, inquiring of God rather than presuming, that Saul so fatally lacked. It is a study in what faithful kingship looks like, pointing forward to the true King who never acted apart from His Father's will and whom God has now highly exalted above all.

context.literary:
Read against its source, this chapter reveals something distinctive about how the Chronicler builds his narrative. Nearly every verse here matches 2 Samuel 5:11-25 almost word for word, yet in Samuel this material appears before David ever attempts to move the ark, while the Chronicler relocates it to sit between the ark's failed and corrected journeys. The material itself has not changed; its position has. That relocation is a deliberate literary choice, not a chronological correction, and it turns straightforward historical reporting into commentary: David's house building, his family's growth, and his battlefield victories are now framed on both sides by his handling of the ark, so that every mark of David's success reads as flowing from, and answerable to, his pursuit of God's presence rather than standing as an achievement in its own right.

The chapter itself has a tight, repetitive shape built around two battles that mirror each other in outline, a Philistine raid, an inquiry of God, an answer, a victory, yet differ sharply in content, a direct advance the first time, verses 8-12, a flanking maneuver commanded down to a specific auditory signal the second, verses 13-17. That deliberate repetition with variation is the chapter's central literary device: it trains the reader to expect the pattern of inquiry itself, not the particular content of any single answer, as the real lesson.

Even the opening genealogical list of sons born in Jerusalem, verses 4-7, functions as more than a record; set right after the note that the LORD had exalted David's kingdom, it visibly displays that exaltation in the plainest terms available to an ancient reader, a growing house and a growing name, before the chapter turns to prove the same point on the battlefield.
context.historical:
The Valley of Rephaim ran southwest from Jerusalem toward Bethlehem, close enough to the new capital that a Philistine force camped there posed a direct and immediate threat, not a distant border matter; Isaiah later uses the same valley as a byword for sudden, overwhelming intervention against a harvest, Isaiah 17:5. The balsam trees of verse 14, whose exact identity even the ancient translators disputed, mattered less for their botany than for the tactical instruction attached to them: David was to wait until he heard the sound of marching in the tops before advancing, a signal apparently meant as evidence that the LORD Himself, not David's own timing, had already engaged the enemy first.

Burning captured enemy images, verse 12, was not incidental piety but obedience to explicit Mosaic command: Israel was to burn the carved images of the gods it defeated rather than keep, sell, or even bring the silver and gold off them into its own houses, Deuteronomy 7:25. That the Philistines abandoned their gods in their retreat, leaving behind the very objects they trusted for victory, would have struck an ancient audience as a public humiliation of those gods' claimed power, not merely a battlefield detail.

Hiram's gift of cedar and craftsmen also marks Tyre's timber and stonework as a recognized regional luxury; the same Phoenician resources and skill would be sought again a generation later for Solomon's temple, 2 Chronicles 2:3, 8, 16, linking David's palace and Solomon's temple as parallel achievements resting on the same foreign alliance.
context.canonical:
The phrase 'David realized that the LORD had established him,' verse 2, belongs to a small but significant biblical pattern in which a king comes to recognize, sometimes suddenly, that his throne rests entirely on a power not his own; compare Nebuchadnezzar's confession after his humbling, that the Most High is sovereign over the kingdoms of men, Daniel 4:32, and Solomon's own prayer crediting the LORD alone for his father's and his own throne, 1 Kings 8:15-20. Chronicles is unusually interested in kings who see this clearly, since the whole book is asking its readers to see the same thing about their own restored, fragile community.

The burning of the Philistines' abandoned gods, verse 12, anticipates the sustained prophetic mockery of idols that cannot save their own worshipers, let alone deliver them from battle, a theme Isaiah develops at length, Isaiah 46:1-2, where Babylon's own gods must be carried away as burdens rather than carrying anyone. And David's spreading fame among all nations, verse 17, plants a small seed that the prophets later grow into full flower: a day when the LORD's name will be great among the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting, Malachi 1:11, fame no longer limited to reports of a victorious king but belonging to the LORD Himself, worshiped everywhere.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The Chronicler positions this chapter to answer a question his first readers were bound to ask after chapter 13's disaster: is David, and by extension Israel's whole restored community, capable of getting anything right? His answer is carefully calibrated. Yes, when the specific matter at hand is inquiring of God before acting, David succeeds completely, twice, in exact contrast to Saul, whose fatal failure to inquire was named just three chapters earlier, 10:13-14. The author wants his readers to see that success with God is not about achieving flawless performance across every area of life at once, David has, after all, just failed badly with the ark, but about cultivating a specific, repeatable posture of dependence that can be practiced consistently even while other lessons are still being learned the hard way. He is teaching a returning, uncertain community that they do not need to have everything sorted out before God will honor their inquiry; they need only actually ask.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter records that God gave David detailed, situation specific battle instructions, down to a precise sound cue in the treetops; it does not promise that every believer who prays before a decision will receive comparably explicit, tactical direction. Modern readers who expect an audible battle plan for every choice risk missing what the text is actually holding up as exemplary, which is not the content of the guidance but David's refusal to act without seeking it first, twice, even after the first inquiry had already proved reliable. What transfers as abiding instruction is the discipline of asking before assuming, particularly when a new situation merely resembles, rather than exactly repeats, one already faced; what does not transfer is any expectation that God's answers must always arrive in the same form, or that faithful dependence guarantees an easy or immediate victory.

debates.question: Why did David inquire of God separately for what looks like the same battle twice?

views.label: Because circumstances and God's plan had genuinely changed
views.case: The second Philistine raid, though in the same valley, required a different tactic, circling around and attacking from the balsam trees rather than a direct advance, showing that God's specific guidance for one situation should never be presumed to apply automatically to the next, even a similar one.

views.label: To model that dependence on God is a discipline, not a one-time decision
views.case: Even after a decisive victory, David does not coast on his prior success or on having heard from God once; he returns to ask again, teaching that faithful dependence is a repeated posture of the heart rather than information banked and reused.

debates.bearing: Both readings converge on the same lesson: David refuses to let a previous answer from God substitute for present inquiry, modeling ongoing rather than one-time dependence.

debates.question: Does David's polygamy in verse 3 receive the narrator's approval?

views.label: A neutral historical note within the honor of the moment
views.case: The verse simply records what happened as part of David's growing household and dynasty, in keeping with the royal customs of the era, without explicit narratorial judgment either way.

views.label: A quiet foreshadowing of trouble, in tension with Deuteronomy's warning
views.case: Deuteronomy 17:17 explicitly warns that the king 'must not take many wives,' and Chronicles elsewhere shows the painful fruit of David's household complications; even without an explicit rebuke here, an alert reader of the Law would sense the warning signs.

debates.bearing: The Chronicler's focus in this chapter is David's dependence on God in battle, not a verdict on his domestic life, but the wider canon does not let readers treat verse 3 as simply commendable.

study.originalLanguages:
Two roots do the heavy lifting in this chapter, and one of them reaches back with real force to the story just told. When David cries out after his first victory, 'Like a bursting flood, God has burst out against my enemies by my hand,' verse 11, the verb is parats, precisely the root that named Perez-uzzah two chapters earlier, the place of outbreak where judgment fell on careless hands. Here the same root describes an outbreak of the opposite kind, sudden, decisive, victorious, and entirely credited to God rather than to David's own hand. The wordplay is almost certainly deliberate: the same root that once marked judgment against presumption now marks deliverance for a king who has learned, this time, to ask first. David even names the battlefield Baal-perazim, fixing the very same Hebrew root permanently onto the landscape a second time within two chapters, but with an entirely different meaning attached to it.

The verb kun, to establish or make firm, stands behind 'the LORD had established him as king,' verse 2, a root used elsewhere of laying an immovable foundation, Psalm 24:2, and of Solomon's throne being made firm after him, 1 Kings 2:12. Paired with nasa, lifted or exalted, already noted in the lexicon, the verse describes David's kingship in the vocabulary of construction and elevation together, founded from beneath and raised from above, language that will resurface even more explicitly when God promises to build David a house, bayit, in the next chapter's covenant, 17:10-14.

David's second inquiry receives an answer built on the rare word tsa'adah, marching or stepping, verse 15, a term used almost nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible outside this scene and its parallel, 2 Samuel 5:24, describing footsteps or a marching sound heard from above rather than seen. Paired with it is the ordinary verb yatsa, has gone out, the usual word for a general marching out to war, but applied here to the LORD Himself: God has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines. Israel's holy wars regularly picture the LORD as a warrior who goes out ahead of His army, Judges 4:14, Deuteronomy 20:4, and this scene gives that picture an audible, almost eerie, confirmation, footsteps overhead before a single Israelite sword is drawn.

Twice more, darash threads the chapter together, appearing at verses 10 and 14 in nearly identical form, David inquired of God, then David again inquired of God, a repetition so exact that it reads almost like a refrain, driving home by sheer verbal repetition the very discipline the Chronicler wants his readers to notice and imitate.

typology.type: David inquiring of God before every battle rather than presuming on his own strength
typology.fulfillment: Twice in one chapter David refuses to act on assumption, even a recent, decisive victory, and stops instead to ask what God would have him do. Jesus takes this same posture to its limit and beyond, doing nothing by Himself but only what He sees the Father doing, seeking not His own will but the will of Him who sent Him, John 5:19, 30. David's dependence, real as it is, remains partial, since the very same chapter records him taking more wives without any recorded inquiry, verse 3, a decision Deuteronomy 17:17 already warns against. Christ's dependence knows no such gap.

typology.type: The LORD highly exalting David's kingdom for the sake of His people
typology.fulfillment: God raises David's kingdom, verse 2, not for David's own glory but explicitly for Israel's good, an exaltation given away rather than kept. Paul takes up strikingly similar language for Jesus, whom God highly exalted and gave the name above every name, precisely because of His humble, obedient death, and precisely to the glory of God the Father, Philippians 2:8-11. David's exaltation, tied from the start to another people's benefit, is a small, historical rehearsal of a far greater exaltation that is given, again, entirely for others' sake rather than claimed for its own.

typology.type: God going out before David's army, signaled by sound in the treetops, before Israel strikes a single blow
typology.fulfillment: David is told to wait for evidence that the LORD has already engaged the enemy before he ever advances, a pattern of victory won by divine initiative before human effort joins it. That pattern reaches its fullest expression at the cross and resurrection, where the powers and authorities were disarmed and triumphed over before any believer took up a single spiritual battle at all, Colossians 2:15. Just as David's task was simply to follow where God had already gone, believers are called to stand firm in a victory already secured rather than to win one of their own making, Ephesians 6:10-13.

study.christ:
This chapter reaches toward Christ mainly through pattern rather than direct promise, and the pattern is dependence itself. Twice David refuses to act on assumption, even a very reasonable assumption built on a recent, decisive victory, and instead stops to ask God directly what to do. Scripture elsewhere treats this kind of dependence as rare and costly; Saul's whole reign collapses partly because he would not do it, 10:13-14, and Israel's kings after David rarely manage it consistently either. David's double inquiry here stands out precisely because it is so unusual, which is what makes it worth reading forward toward the one king who did this perfectly and without exception.

Jesus describes His own life in language that reads like David's practice taken to its limit and beyond: the Son can do nothing by Himself, He can only do what He sees His Father doing, John 5:19, and, I do not seek My own will, but the will of Him who sent Me, John 5:30. Where David inquired before two battles in one chapter, Jesus inquired, in effect, before every act of His whole life, with no recorded exception and no recorded failure of nerve. David's dependence, real as it is, remains partial; he still takes multiple wives in the very same chapter, verse 3, a decision Deuteronomy 17:17 already warns kings against, and no inquiry of God is recorded before it. His dependence has no such gap.

The chapter's language of exaltation also points forward. God highly exalted, nasa, David's kingdom for the sake of His people Israel, verse 2, language of a king raised up not for his own glory but for others' good. Paul takes up strikingly similar vocabulary for Jesus, whom God highly exalted and gave the name that is above every name, explicitly because of His humble, obedient death, Philippians 2:8-9, and explicitly to the glory of God the Father, Philippians 2:11, exaltation given entirely for others' sake rather than claimed for one's own. David's exaltation, tied to Israel's good, is a small, historical instance of a much larger pattern that reaches its full height only in the Son.

Even the burned idols of verse 12 point somewhere. Israel's God proves stronger than the gods the Philistines trusted for victory, gods abandoned on the very battlefield where they were meant to help. Every power hostile to God's people is finally and fully disarmed not on a battlefield near Jerusalem but at the cross, where the powers and authorities were disarmed and triumphed over, Colossians 2:15, the decisive defeat toward which every lesser victory in Israel's story, including this one, was always pointing.
study.god:
God is shown here as the one who actually builds what looks, on the surface, like David's own achievement. A foreign king's cedar and craftsmen, a growing household, two decisive military victories, all of it is credited in the text itself not to David's competence but to the LORD's own hand: David realized that the LORD had established him as king and had highly exalted his kingdom, verse 2. The chapter does not deny that David acted, planned, or fought; it insists that behind every visible cause stood an invisible, prior, sufficient one.

He is also, notably, a God who answers differently depending on the actual situation rather than issuing a single stock response. The first Philistine threat receives a direct, simple answer, go, for I will deliver them into your hand, verse 10; the second, though it looks identical on the surface, a return raid to the same valley, receives an entirely different, more elaborate strategy, a flanking maneuver and a specific audible signal, verses 14-15. This tells readers something important about how God relates to His people: He does not deal in generic formulas applied automatically to similar looking circumstances, but attends to each moment freshly, which is precisely why David has to ask again rather than simply reapplying what worked before.

God's justice toward the nations also surfaces here in a way easy to miss. The Philistines who raided Rephaim are decisively defeated, and their abandoned gods burned, yet Israel is never told to exterminate the Philistine people themselves, and the narrative moves on to fame rather than to further slaughter, verse 17. God's dealings with hostile nations in this chapter are severe toward what threatens His people and what claims false divinity, but they are not indiscriminately destructive of human life beyond the battle itself.

Finally, this chapter reveals God as one who works through means that look, from a human vantage point, almost coincidental, a foreign king's unsolicited gift, a repeated but varied enemy raid, ordinary soldiers, and produces through them an outcome, David's established fame among all nations, verse 17, that only makes sense as the deliberate result of divine intention rather than a string of lucky breaks. The God of this chapter is sovereign over international politics, marriage and family, and the sound of wind in treetops alike, with nothing in David's growing kingdom left outside His active governance.

crossReferences.note: Saul died for his unfaithfulness and because he did not inquire of the LORD, but instead consulted a medium for guidance. This is the exact failure this chapter shows David repeatedly avoiding, and the Chronicler places the two accounts only a few pages apart so the contrast cannot be missed.

The parallel account of these same two Philistine victories, recorded in nearly identical language, though positioned before the ark narrative rather than between its two halves as the Chronicler arranges it. Comparing the two orderings shows how deliberately Chronicles reshapes its source material for theological effect.

The Law's command to burn the carved images of defeated nations' gods rather than keep their silver or gold for personal use, on pain of being ensnared by the very thing that trapped the nations who worshiped it. David's burning of the abandoned gods, verse 12, is direct, careful obedience to this specific instruction.

The LORD causes the Aramean army besieging Samaria to hear the sound of chariots and horses and a great army, and they flee in panic without a single Israelite soldier engaging them. The sound in the balsam treetops here works by the same principle, a divinely produced sound that routs an enemy before human force is even applied.

The law of the king, including the explicit warning that Israel's king must not take many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away. David's multiplying wives in verse 3, recorded without comment here, sits in quiet tension with this command even at a high point of his obedience elsewhere in the chapter.

Jesus describes His own total dependence on the Father, doing nothing of Himself and seeking not His own will but the will of the One who sent Him. This is the pattern David models faithfully but only partially in this chapter, brought here to its complete and unbroken fulfillment.

God highly exalts Jesus and gives Him the name above every name because of His humble, obedient death, so that every knee will bow to the glory of God the Father. The exaltation language echoes verse 2's account of David's own kingdom being highly exalted for the sake of others.

Christ disarms the powers and authorities and triumphs over them through the cross, the final and complete version of the defeat David's God works against the Philistines and their abandoned gods in this chapter's two battles.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 12 promised Abraham that his name would be made great and that he would be a source of blessing to others, a promise this chapter shows beginning to be realized in a small but real way: David's fame went out into every land, verse 17, precisely the kind of international recognition Abraham's descendants were always meant to carry, not for their own sake but for the sake of His people Israel, verse 2. Set between the ark's two journeys, this chapter insists that David's fame and Israel's military security are never the main plot; they are by-products of a king who keeps stopping to ask God what to do, in deliberate, pointed contrast to the very first king, whose refusal to inquire cost him everything, 10:13-14.

The pattern set here, a king who depends rather than presumes, becomes the standard against which every later king in Chronicles is measured, and against which nearly every one of them, David himself included, at points falls short. The whole rest of the book keeps testing this same question: will this king inquire of the LORD, or will he act as though the last answer covers every future situation? Much of Israel's later history, exile among it, traces back to kings who stopped asking.

The story's forward trajectory runs, finally, to the King who never once failed to ask, whose entire life was inquiry answered by perfect obedience, doing nothing of Himself and seeking only His Father's will, John 5:19, 30, and who has therefore been highly exalted above every other name, Philippians 2:9. What David modeled imperfectly, twice, in one chapter of victories soon complicated by his own later failures, Christ fulfilled perfectly across an entire life, and it is His exaltation, not David's fame among the nations, that the whole story has ultimately been building toward.

quiz.q: What does Hiram's gift of cedar and craftsmen signal about David's kingdom?

options.text: That the LORD had established David as king and highly exalted his kingdom, recognized now even by a foreign ruler.
options.note: Verses 1-2 tie Hiram's gift directly to David's realization that the LORD had established and exalted him.

options.text: That David had formed a military alliance to attack the Philistines.
options.note: Hiram's gift concerned building materials and craftsmen for a palace, not a military alliance against the Philistines.

options.text: That David was now wealthy enough to build his own temple.
options.note: The gift built David's palace, not a temple; the temple's construction belongs to Solomon later in the book.

options.text: That Tyre wanted to establish trade routes through Jerusalem.
options.note: Trade and international relations were surely part of the picture, but the text's explicit point is David's recognition that the LORD had established and exalted his kingdom.

quiz.q: What did David do differently from Saul when the Philistines attacked?

options.text: He inquired of God directly before going to battle, both times, rather than acting on assumption or past experience.
options.note: Verses 10 and 14 record David inquiring of God, contrasted with Saul's failure to inquire, 10:14.

options.text: He hired foreign mercenaries to strengthen his army.
options.note: No such hiring is recorded; the contrast the text draws is about inquiring of God, not military recruitment.

options.text: He waited for the Philistines to retreat on their own before engaging.
options.note: David actively went out to face them and later attacked; he did not simply wait for withdrawal.

options.text: He consulted his military commanders before acting.
options.note: David does confer with leaders in the surrounding narrative (13:1), but in this specific chapter the explicit contrast with Saul is about inquiring of God, not human commanders.

quiz.q: How did God answer David's second inquiry differently from the first?

options.text: God gave a detailed tactical plan, circling around to attack from the balsam trees and waiting for the sound of marching in the treetops, rather than a straightforward yes to advance directly.
options.note: Verses 14-15 record this specific, situational guidance, different from the direct 'Go' of verse 10.

options.text: God refused to answer the second time, leaving David to decide alone.
options.note: God answers clearly both times; the second answer includes detailed tactical instructions.

options.text: God told David to retreat and avoid the Philistines entirely.
options.note: God commanded engagement, not retreat, giving specific instructions for how to attack.

options.text: God simply repeated the same instruction as the first battle.
options.note: This understates the difference; the second answer was tactically distinct, requiring a flanking maneuver rather than a direct advance.

quiz.q: What happened to the Philistines' gods after the first battle at Baal-perazim?

options.text: The Philistines abandoned them there, and David ordered them burned in the fire.
options.note: Verse 12 records both the abandonment and David's command to burn them, in obedience to the Law's demand regarding idols, Deuteronomy 7:5, 25.

options.text: David kept them as trophies in his palace.
options.note: The opposite is recorded; David had them destroyed by fire, not kept as trophies.

options.text: The Philistines took their gods with them in retreat.
options.note: The text specifically says the gods were abandoned there, not carried off in retreat.

options.text: The idols were left where they fell without further comment.
options.note: This omits David's explicit command that they be burned, an act of obedience to the Law's demand to destroy idols.

quiz.q: What was the ultimate result of David's two victories over the Philistines?

options.text: David's fame spread into every land, and the LORD caused all nations to fear him.
options.note: Verse 17 records this outcome directly, framing the victories as building David's international reputation under God's hand.

options.text: The Philistines were permanently destroyed as a nation.
options.note: The Philistines remain a recurring threat throughout David's reign and beyond; they were defeated in battle here, not eliminated as a people.

options.text: David was forced to pay tribute to the Philistines afterward.
options.note: The opposite occurred; David defeated the Philistines and gained fame, not the reverse.

options.text: David's kingdom gained territory but no lasting reputation among the nations.
options.note: This understates the outcome; the text specifically highlights the spread of David's fame and the nations' fear of him, not merely territorial gain.

questions: Twice David stopped to inquire of God rather than assuming he knew what to do based on his first victory. Where in your life do you tend to rely on past experience rather than seeking God fresh for what is in front of you now?
God gave David a different, more detailed battle plan the second time. How do you respond when God's guidance for a new situation looks different from how He led you before?
The chapter contrasts David's dependence with Saul's failure to inquire of the LORD. What would it look like this week to build the simple habit of asking God before acting, rather than after?

David gave God credit, even naming the battlefield after what God had done, 'God has burst out against my enemies.' Where could you be more deliberate in giving God the credit for victories in your own life?

God's stated purpose in exalting David was 'for the sake of His people Israel,' not David's personal glory. How does remembering that your own gifts and successes are meant to serve others shape the way you use them?

translationNotes.note: Shammua is a BSB-noted variant of Shimea, 1 Chronicles 3:5; the same son appears under both names in Chronicles' genealogies.
Beeliada is a BSB-noted variant of Eliada, the same son named in the parallel list, 2 Samuel 5:16.
Baal-perazim means 'the LORD bursts out,' per the BSB footnote, David's own naming of the site after God's decisive victory there.
The BSB footnote allows 'balsam trees' to be rendered aspen or poplar trees; the identity of the tree is uncertain, but the sense of the tactical instruction is unaffected.
